docs.text:
Item Shortcut What it does Documentation F1 This documentation, in a window of its own, without a network connection Documentation Online The same documentation on the website Sample Charts… A file dialog in your samples folder: pick a ready-made chart to open Sample Datasets… A file dialog in your sample datasets folder: pick one or more files to load Licenses This documentation, on the page with the licence of plotviz and of the packages it contains About plotviz The version, the copyright and the licence, with a Licenses… button that opens the same page

The samples are copies of the examples that come with plotviz, made the first time it runs, so you can open and change them freely. They live in the plots and datasets folders of the config folder shown in the Preferences. (A pip install does not include them; the binary releases and a source checkout do.) The sample charts cover each chart type; the sample datasets are the data behind them, and some more to try the Generate, Transform and Statistics pages (pulse_signal.csv, fit_test.csv, dates_daily.csv…).

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text:
plotviz → Preferences… (Ctrl + ,) on macOS, Edit → Settings… (Ctrl + Alt + S) on Windows and Linux.

  1. Configuration files — Where plotviz keeps the settings file, the config folder, and the folders of your colour schemes and palettes. A button next to each opens its folder.
  2. Appearance — Colour scheme: System, Light or Dark. It is applied at once, and Cancel puts it back.
  3. Defaults — Show navigation toolbar (the matplotlib toolbar above the chart) and Max recent files (1 to 30).
  4. Maintenance — Clear recent files, and Reset all settings to defaults…, which does not touch your charts or data.

docs.title: Color Palettes
docs.text: A color palette is an ordered list of 16 colors used as the default cycle for series in a chart. When a new series is added, the next color in the active palette is assigned automatically.

docs.title: Selecting a palette
docs.text: In the Layout & Style tab, choose a palette from the Color palette dropdown. The chart updates immediately, reassigning colors to all series that do not have a locked color.

docs.title: Built-in palettes
docs.text:
plotviz ships with 11 palettes:

Name Character Matplotlib The standard matplotlib default color cycle — blue, orange, green, red, purple, brown, pink, grey, yellow-green, cyan Pastel Soft, desaturated tones — baby blue, peach, mint, rose, periwinkle Bold High-contrast vivid colors — red, green, blue, orange, purple, cyan, magenta, lime Earth Warm browns, greens and greys — saddle brown, olive, khaki, forest green Ocean Deep cool blues through warm orange — navy, indigo, purple, magenta, coral, amber Warm Reds, oranges and yellows — crimson, tangerine, gold, coral, amber Cool Blues, greens and purples — steel blue, teal, sage, lavender, sky Colorblind Optimized for the most common forms of color vision deficiency (deuteranopia, protanopia) Nature Muted greens, blues and earthy tones — teal, burnt orange, coral, dark blue Publication Black + strong, distinct hues suitable for print — black, red, blue, green, purple, orange Grayscale Black through white in even steps — for monochrome print or accessibility

docs.title: Custom palettes
docs.text: Palettes work like colour schemes: the built-in ones are read-only, and your own are files. Every .pvizp in the palettes folder is loaded when plotviz starts. Its location is shown in Preferences (Colour palettes), next to a button that opens it; on macOS it is ~/Library/Application Support/plotviz/palettes/.

docs.title: Creating or editing a palette
docs.text:
1. In the Layout & Style tab, click Edit palette…. It opens with the colours of the active palette; Load from starts from another one.
  2. Give it a name and click each of the 16 swatches to set the colours.
  3. Click Save & apply. The palette becomes the active one.

Opening the editor on one of your own palettes edits it in place. Built-in names cannot be replaced.

A * after a palette's name in the dropdown means it is not in the palettes folder, so it will not be there next time. A new palette starts that way; saving it into the folder removes the *.

docs.title: Sharing and keeping palettes
docs.text:
Save: click Save under Colour palette. The dialog opens in the palettes folder; you can save anywhere else too, but a file outside the folder keeps its * and is not loaded at start-up. Built-in palettes cannot be saved, since they are always there. To delete a palette, delete its file.

Load: click Load and choose a single .pvizp file (for instance one from outside the folder). With one palette in the file you are asked whether to apply it.

A chart file (.pviz) carries its active palette when it is one of yours, so the chart opens with the same colours.

docs.title: Re-applying the palette
docs.text:
Series whose colour you set by hand keep it when you change palette or scheme. ↺ Re-apply palette (under the Edit / Load / Save buttons) gives every series its palette colour again, those included.

See File Formats for the .pvizp format specification.

docs.title: Color locking
docs.text:
By default, switching palettes reassigns all series colors to match the new palette. To preserve a specific series' color across palette switches, tick Lock color in the Series tab for that series.

Locked colors are shown with a lock icon in the series color swatch. They are never modified by palette changes, but can still be changed manually by clicking the swatch.

docs.title: Recent colors in the color picker
docs.text: The color picker dialog shows a Recent colors row above the Custom colors section. It stores the last 8 colors you selected (across all color pickers in the app) and persists them between sessions. Click any recent swatch to instantly reuse that color.

docs.title: Plot: Series and Chart Types
docs.text: The Plots → Plot page decides what is drawn: which columns, as which chart type, in which subplot. Everything else about how it looks is on the other pages of the Plots tab.

docs.title: The series table
docs.text:
The series table is on the Plots → Plot page:

  1. Plot mode — Which group of chart types the subplot uses: Standard, Histogram, Statistical, Heatmap & Contour, Polar & Radar, Pie or Quiver.
  2. Series — One row per plotted series: the X and Y columns, the legend Label, the chart Type, the number of the subplot it belongs to (Plot) and whether it uses the secondary axis (Y2). Add series and Remove selected change the rows. Below the table, the options of the selected series appear.
Column Purpose X Column used as the horizontal axis values Y Column used as the vertical axis values Label Text shown in the chart legend Type Chart type for this series (Line, Scatter, Bar, …) Plot Which subplot panel this series appears in (1-based) Y2 Checkbox — plots this series on the secondary Y axis

docs.title: Adding and removing series
docs.text:
• + Add series — appends a new row with empty column selections.
  • − Remove selected — removes the selected rows.

docs.title: Mixing chart types
docs.text:
Each row in the series table has its own Type dropdown, so you can mix chart types within the same panel — for example, a Line series and a Scatter series sharing the same axes.

Types that take over the whole chart (Histogram, Pie, Heatmap, etc.) cannot be mixed with other types in the same subplot.

docs.title: Secondary Y axis (Y2)
docs.text: Tick the Y2 checkbox on any series row to plot it against a second Y axis on the right side of the chart. The Y2 axis label is set in the Axes tab.

docs.title: Z column and error column
docs.text:
Below the series table are two extra dropdowns:

  • Z — used by Heatmap, Hist2D, Hexbin, Contour, and Bubble charts as the third data dimension.
  • Error — used by the Errorbar chart as the error/uncertainty values.

docs.title: Chart type selection
docs.text:
The Plot mode dropdown at the top of Plots → Plot chooses a group of chart types for the subplot: Standard, Histogram, Statistical, Heatmap & Contour, Polar & Radar, Pie or Quiver. The Type cell of each series offers the types of that group.

In Standard the type belongs to each series, so they can be mixed; the other groups draw the whole panel as one chart.

See Chart Types for a full description of every chart type and its options.

docs.title: Python Export Bundle
docs.text: The Python Export Bundle feature converts any plotviz chart into a self-contained Python project — a ZIP archive (.pvizx) that includes a standalone matplotlib script and the chart's data as CSV files. The exported script has no dependency on plotviz and can be run, shared, and modified in any Python environment.

docs.title: Save to file
docs.text:
Go to File → Export Python Bundle (.pvizx)… (or use the corresponding menu shortcut).

A save dialog appears with a suggested filename based on the current chart title. Choose a location and click Save.

After the export completes, a confirmation message shows the full file path. The bundle can be extracted and run immediately:

unzip mychart.pvizx -d mychart
cd mychart
python plot.py

docs.title: Send directly to Code Runner
docs.text: Use Tools → Code Runner from chart (or the ▶ Open in Code Runner button in the Seaborn Explorer) to skip the save dialog entirely. plotviz writes the bundle to a temporary location and opens it in the Python Code Runner so you can inspect and edit the generated script right away.

docs.title: Bundle contents
docs.text:
A .pvizx file is a standard ZIP archive with the following structure:

mychart.pvizx
├── plot.py          # Standalone matplotlib script
├── README.md        # Quick-start instructions
├── pyproject.toml   # Optional: dependency declaration
└── data/
    ├── data.csv     # All columns (when they share the same length)
    │   — or —
    ├── column1.csv  # One CSV per column (when lengths differ)
    └── column2.csv

docs.title: plot.py
docs.text:
The main script is completely standalone — it imports only standard scientific Python packages and reads its data from the data/ folder relative to its own location. It faithfully reproduces:

  • All chart types and subplot layouts
  • Axis labels, limits, scales, and tick formatting
  • Series colors, line widths, markers, and fill styles
  • Curve fits with optional confidence and prediction bands
  • Title, legend, grid, and figure size

docs.title: data/
docs.text: Date columns are written to the CSV as ISO 8601 text (2024-03-01, 2024-03-01T12:30:00), and the script converts them back with pd.to_datetime, so the exported chart has a date axis too. Only the columns actually assigned to series in the chart are exported. If all exported columns share the same row count, they are written to a single data/data.csv. If they differ in length, each column gets its own CSV file (e.g. data/pressure.csv) to avoid NaN padding.

docs.title: pyproject.toml
docs.text: A minimal pyproject.toml listing the required packages (matplotlib, numpy, pandas, scipy) for use with tools like uv or pip.

docs.title: Running the exported script
docs.text:
Requirements (installed automatically if using pyproject.toml):

pip install matplotlib numpy pandas scipy

Then run:

python plot.py

The chart is displayed in a matplotlib window. To save it instead, call plt.savefig('output.png', dpi=300) at the end of the script.

docs.title: Opening a .pvizx bundle
docs.text:
You can re-open any .pvizx file in the Python Code Runner to edit the generated script interactively:

  1. Open the Code Runner: Tools → Python Code Runner…
  2. Click 📦 Load .pvizx… and select the bundle.
  3. plotviz extracts the archive, loads plot.py into the editor, and runs it automatically.

You can also double-click a .pvizx file in Finder (macOS) or Explorer (Windows) to open it directly in the Code Runner, if plotviz is set as the default application for that file type.

docs.title: Supported chart types
docs.text:
All 22 plotviz chart types are supported in the Python export, including:

Line, Scatter, Step, Area, Bar, Stem, Error Bar, Histogram, Boxplot, Violin, Pie, Polar, Radar, Heatmap, Contour, Tricontour, 3D Surface, ECDF, 2D Histogram, Hexbin, Quiver, Barbs, Streamplot

Seaborn charts created in the Seaborn Explorer can be exported via the 🐍 Generate Python Code or ▶ Open in Code Runner buttons in that dialog.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The exported script uses absolute file paths resolved relative to plot.py, so keep plot.py and the data/ folder together.
  • plotviz-specific features like drag-and-drop annotations and the manual data table are reproduced in the script as static data.
  • The .pvizx extension is not a standard zip alias on all platforms — use an explicit unzip command or a ZIP tool if double-clicking does not extract it outside of plotviz.

docs.title: Seaborn Explorer
docs.text:
The Seaborn Explorer is a dedicated dialog for creating statistical charts powered by seaborn. It runs on its own canvas, fully isolated from the main plotviz chart, so figure-level seaborn plots (Pairplot, Joint, Heatmap, Catplot) never interfere with the main chart's style pipeline.

Open it from the menu bar: Tools → Seaborn Explorer…

Requirements

Seaborn must be installed: pip install seaborn. Some regression options (Robust fit, LOWESS) additionally require pip install statsmodels.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
The window, from left to right and top to bottom:

  1. Chart type — One of the eight types below; a line under the box describes it.
  2. Color theme — The palette: plotviz uses the palette of the current chart, the others are seaborn palettes.
  3. Data columns — The columns for X, Y and, for some types, Hue, Size and Style. Heatmap and Pairplot show a list of columns to pick instead.
  4. Chart options — The options of the chosen type. This box changes with the type (see below).
  5. Canvas toolbar — The matplotlib tools: home, back and forward, pan, zoom, subplot settings, axis editor and save.
  6. Preview — The chart. Changes to the controls are drawn when you click Redraw.
  7. Bottom bar — Redraw, the export DPI, Export…, Generate Python Code, Open in Code Runner and Close.

The window has two panels:

Panel Contents Left — controls Chart type, color theme, column selectors, and chart-specific options Right — preview Live seaborn canvas with navigation toolbar and export controls

Changes to the controls do not redraw automatically — click Redraw to apply them.

docs.title: Chart types
docs.text: Type Description KDE Kernel Density Estimate — smoothed distribution curve Regression Scatter plot with OLS, polynomial, or LOWESS regression line Strip Categorical scatter plot with jitter Swarm Categorical beeswarm plot (non-overlapping points) Heatmap Correlation matrix heatmap Pairplot All-vs-all scatter grid (uses column picker) Joint Bivariate joint distribution with marginals Catplot Figure-level categorical chart (box, violin, bar, strip, and more)

docs.title: What each type draws
docs.text:
The pictures use the tips and penguins sample datasets of the seaborn collection (in the seaborn folder of the sample datasets).

KDE — the smoothed distribution of one column (here total_bill).

Regression — tip against total_bill, with the fitted line and its 95 % confidence band.

Strip — total_bill for each day, one dot per bill, spread sideways (jitter) so they do not hide each other.

Swarm — tip for each day, with the dots moved aside so that none overlaps.

Heatmap — the correlation between the numeric columns of the penguins sample, with the values written in the cells (Annotate).

Pairplot — every pair of the numeric columns, coloured by species (Hue).

Joint — flipper_length_mm against bill_length_mm, with the distribution of each at the sides.

Catplot — a box plot of total_bill by day (Kind: box; the other kinds are boxen, violin, bar, point, count, strip and swarm).

docs.title: Data columns
docs.text:
For chart types that use X/Y axes (KDE, Regression, Strip, Swarm, Joint, Catplot), select columns from the dropdowns:

Dropdown Accepts X column Any loaded column (numeric or categorical) Y column Numeric columns only Hue (category) Categorical columns — splits data into color groups Size (category) Categorical columns — varies marker size by group Style (category) Categorical columns — varies marker shape/line style by group

For Heatmap and Pairplot, a multi-select column list replaces the X/Y dropdowns. Use All / None buttons to quickly select or deselect all numeric columns.

docs.title: Color theme
docs.text:
The Palette dropdown controls the color scheme used for all chart types. The first option, plotviz, applies your current plotviz color palette. All other options are standard seaborn/matplotlib named palettes:

deep, muted, pastel, bright, dark, colorblind, tab10, Set1, Set2, Set3, Paired, husl, hls, rocket, mako, flare, crest, viridis, plasma, magma, inferno

docs.title: KDE options
docs.text: Option Description Fill alpha Opacity of the shaded area under the curve (0–1) Line width Thickness of the KDE line BW adjust Bandwidth smoothing multiplier (higher = smoother) Fill Toggle the shaded fill under the curve Cumulative Show the cumulative distribution instead Common norm Normalize across all hue groups (areas sum to 1 globally)

docs.title: Regression options
docs.text:
Option Description Poly order Polynomial degree for the regression line (1 = linear) CI % Confidence interval width (0–99%) Marker size Scatter point size Alpha Scatter point opacity Robust fit Use robust regression (requires statsmodels) LOWESS Non-parametric locally-weighted smoothing (requires statsmodels) Show scatter Toggle the underlying scatter points

Note

Robust fit and LOWESS are mutually exclusive with each other and with polynomial order > 1.

docs.title: Regression here and in Curves
docs.text:
The Explorer draws a trend line over the points, to look at them. The curve fit of Plots → Curves (see Curves and Fitting) fits a model that you can read numbers from, compare and keep with the chart. They are not two versions of the same tool:

Explorer → Regression Plots → Curves → Curve fit What it is A picture for exploring the data A fit that is stored in the chart Models A line or a polynomial (order 1 to 6), a robust line, or LOWESS Linear, polynomial up to degree 10, exponential (with or without an offset), power, logarithmic, sigmoid, Gaussian, sinusoid, your own expression, and LOWESS Band CI % (95 by default), found by resampling the data at random; it is not drawn for a robust fit or for LOWESS Confidence limits and Prediction band, at 1, 2 or 3 sigma, calculated from the uncertainty of the parameters Numbers None The equation, the parameters with their errors, R², adjusted R², RMSE, AIC, BIC and, for the models where it applies, an F-test; they can be exported to a text file Outliers Robust fit lessens their weight Robust lessens their weight and marks the points that stand out, counting them in the results Part of the data All the points Fit only x from … to … fits one stretch Weights No Weight by the error column Comparing No: Redraw replaces the chart The Fits list keeps several fits of a series, with R² and AIC side by side Where it lives In the Explorer window; it leaves as an image or as a script On the main chart, saved in the .pviz and in the exported script New data None New series with the curve and the bands, which can be drawn or transformed

When to use which: the Explorer to see quickly whether there is a trend, or for a fast figure with the seaborn look; Curves when you need a value (the slope and its uncertainty), want to compare models, fit only part of the data, or keep the fit with the chart.

Two details. The straight line is the same in both (a least-squares line), but the Explorer's band comes from random resampling, so it changes a little each time the chart is redrawn, whereas the band of Curves is calculated and always the same. And LOWESS is in both only to show a trend, with no equation: in the Explorer it is drawn over the points, in Curves it joins the Fits list and is saved with the chart.

docs.title: Strip options
docs.text: Option Description Marker size Point size Alpha Point opacity Jitter Amount of random horizontal spread to reduce overplotting (0–0.5)

docs.title: Swarm options
docs.text: Option Description Marker size Point size Alpha Point opacity

docs.title: Heatmap options
docs.text: Option Description Colormap Color scale (coolwarm, viridis, plasma, RdBu, Blues, Reds, YlOrRd, magma, rocket, mako) Format Number format for cell annotations (.2f, .1f, .0f, .2g, d, or blank) Line width Width of the cell border lines Annotate cells Show correlation values inside each cell Square cells Force square cell aspect ratio Show colorbar Show the color scale legend Robust scale Use percentile-based color mapping to reduce outlier influence

docs.title: Pairplot options
docs.text: Option Description Diagonal Plot type for the diagonal (auto, hist, kde) Off-diagonal Plot type for off-diagonal cells (scatter, kde, hist, reg) Alpha Point opacity

docs.title: Joint plot options
docs.text: Option Description Kind Joint plot type (scatter, kde, hist, hex, reg, resid) Alpha Opacity Ratio Size ratio of the joint plot to the marginal plots Marginal KDE fill Fill the marginal KDE distributions

docs.title: Catplot options
docs.text: Option Description Kind Categorical plot type (box, boxen, violin, bar, point, count, strip, swarm) Alpha Opacity Saturation Color saturation (0.1–1.0) CI Confidence interval for bar/point plots (95, 99, sd, or None) Dodge groups Separate hue groups side-by-side instead of overlapping

docs.title: Canvas controls
docs.text: The matplotlib navigation toolbar above the preview canvas provides pan, zoom, and reset controls. See Keyboard Shortcuts for details.

docs.title: Bottom bar
docs.text: Button Description Redraw Re-render the chart with the current control values DPI spinner Export resolution (72–600 DPI) Export… Save the chart as PNG, SVG, PDF, or JPEG 🐍 Generate Python Code Show a standalone Python script that reproduces the current chart ▶ Open in Code Runner Export the chart as a .pvizx bundle and open it in the Python Code Runner Close Close the Seaborn Explorer

docs.title: Generating Python code
docs.text:
Click 🐍 Generate Python Code to view a standalone Python script that reproduces the current seaborn chart without any dependency on plotviz. You can copy and paste this script into any Python environment.

Click ▶ Open in Code Runner to send the chart directly to the Python Code Runner, where you can edit and re-run the generated code interactively.

docs.title: Global shortcuts
docs.text: Shortcut Action Ctrl + N New chart Ctrl + O Open chart Ctrl + S Save chart (rewrites the open file; asks where the first time) Ctrl + Shift + S Save chart as… Ctrl + L Load data Ctrl + E Export image Ctrl + Shift + E Export Python bundle Ctrl + Z Undo Ctrl + Y or Ctrl + Shift + Z Redo Ctrl + Shift + C Copy the chart as an image (Ctrl + C keeps copying text in fields and tables) Ctrl + , (macOS) / Ctrl + Alt + S Preferences / Settings Ctrl + Shift + B Seaborn Explorer Ctrl + Shift + P Python Code Runner Ctrl + Shift + R Code Runner from the current chart F1 Documentation (opens in its own window; Help → Documentation Online opens the website)

docs.title: Tab navigation (View menu)
docs.text:
The View menu lists the three tabs as checkable items; the active one is ticked.

Menu item Tab View → Data Datasets, Generate, Statistics and Transform pages View → Layout & Style Figure size, margins, title, subplot grid, colour scheme, palette View → Plots Per-subplot settings: Plot, Curves, Axes, Canvas & Grid, Legend & Notes

docs.title: Undo and redo
docs.text:
Edit → Undo and Redo (and the two buttons in the top bar) step through up to 50 changes. Hover over a button to see what it will undo or redo ("Undo: Apply fit"), and the status bar says what was undone.

A step is recorded about half a second after the last change, so a burst of edits (typing, dragging a spin box) is one step. Everything that makes up the chart is in it:

  • every setting, per subplot, including the style of each curve;
  • the datasets (loading, removing, Generate, Transform, the data table);
  • the series table and the fits (with their bands, and whether each is shown);
  • the annotations (adding, moving, editing, deleting).

After an undo you stay on the same subplot and curve, and the lists keep their selection. Undo does not cover zooming or panning with the toolbar, the open/save state of the file, or the palettes you saved to disk.

The history starts again when you open a file or start a new chart. The datasets in the history are not copied: a step only holds the arrays that changed, so a long history does not multiply the memory used by large data.

docs.title: Canvas (matplotlib toolbar)
docs.text:
The toolbar above the chart canvas provides standard matplotlib navigation:

Button Action 🏠 Home Reset to the original view ◀ Back Go to the previous view ▶ Forward Go to the next view ✛ Pan Click and drag to pan; right-drag to zoom 🔍 Zoom Draw a rectangle to zoom in ⚙ Subplots Adjust subplot spacing (matplotlib built-in) 💾 Save Save the figure via matplotlib's own dialog

docs.title: Reading values from the chart
docs.text: Move the pointer close to a point of a curve or a scatter plot (within about 14 pixels) and the status bar at the bottom of the window shows the series and the x and y of that point, not those of the pointer: Quadratic · x = 4.5, y = 6.1. On a date axis the value is written as a date. The text disappears when the pointer moves away from the points. Clicking on an empty part of the chart still writes the coordinates of the click.

docs.title: Annotation mode shortcuts
docs.text:
While in the Legend & Notes tab:

Key Action Esc Exit the current annotation placement mode and return to Normal/Drag

docs.title: Color picker
docs.text: Key Action Enter Confirm the selected color (OK) Esc Cancel and close the color picker

docs.title: Series click-to-select
docs.text: Click directly on a plotted series in the canvas to jump to the Series tab with that series pre-selected. This works for line, scatter, bar, and most other series types.

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text: The Data → Statistics page summarises the loaded series. To create new series from them, see Transform.

docs.title: The Statistics page
docs.text:
The Statistics page summarises the loaded series. It works on the series selected in the Datasets list, or on all of them when none is selected. It refreshes when you open the page; click ↻ Refresh after changing the selection or the data.

The Statistics page:

  1. Summary — A table with count, missing values, mean, standard deviation, minimum, quartiles and more, one column per series (the ones selected in the Datasets list, or all of them).
  2. Correlation — The correlation matrix of the series, with the Method (Pearson or Spearman). Refresh recalculates and Copy summary puts the table on the clipboard.

docs.title: Summary table
docs.text:
One column per series and one row per statistic:

Statistic Meaning count Valid values (NaN and infinity are not counted) missing NaN, infinity or empty values mean, std Mean and sample standard deviation (n − 1) min, 25%, median, 75%, max Range and quartiles skew, kurtosis Skewness and excess kurtosis (a normal distribution has 0 for both)

Text series only get count and missing. For date series the mean, minimum, quartiles, median and maximum are shown as dates, and the standard deviation is in days. Cells that cannot be computed (the std of one value, the skew of a constant series) are left blank.

📋 Copy summary copies the table to the clipboard, tab-separated, ready to paste into a spreadsheet.

docs.title: Correlation matrix
docs.text:
Below the summary, the correlation between every pair of numeric series, with cells shaded red for positive and blue for negative values. Choose the Method:

  • pearson — linear correlation.
  • spearman — rank correlation; detects any monotonic relationship, linear or not, and is less sensitive to outliers.

Each pair uses only the points where both series are valid. A cell is blank when the two series have different lengths, one of them is constant, or there are fewer than 3 common points.

docs.title: Subplots
docs.text: plotviz supports multi-panel layouts with up to 9 subplots per chart. Each subplot is an independent axes with its own series, title, labels, limits, legend, and annotations.

docs.title: Opening the layout dialog
docs.text: In the Layout & Style tab, click ⚙️ Configure Subplot Layout… to open the layout picker.

docs.title: Layout presets
docs.text: The Presets tab shows a visual gallery of 18 built-in layouts. Click a preview thumbnail to select it; the chart updates immediately.

docs.title: Regular grids
docs.text: Preset Description Single 1 × 1 (default) 1 × 2 One row, two columns 1 × 3 One row, three columns 2 × 1 Two rows, one column 2 × 2 Two rows, two columns 2 × 3 Two rows, three columns 3 × 1 Three rows, one column 3 × 2 Three rows, two columns 3 × 3 Three rows, three columns

docs.title: Mosaic presets (unequal panels)
docs.text: Preset Description 1 top / 2 down Wide panel on top, two panels below 2 top / 1 down Two panels on top, wide panel below 1 left / 2 right Tall panel on the left, two panels stacked on the right 2 left / 1 right Two panels stacked on the left, tall panel on the right 1 top / 3 down Wide panel on top, three panels in a row below 3 top / 1 down Three panels in a row on top, wide panel below 2×2 mosaic 1+1+2 Two equal panels above, one wide panel below 3 rows / 1 wide top Three rows: wide top, two-column middle, two-column bottom 3 rows / 1 wide bottom Three rows: two-column top, two-column middle, wide bottom

docs.title: Custom mosaic editor
docs.text:
The Custom mosaic tab provides a grid editor for building any layout.

  1. Set the Rows and Columns spinboxes to define the grid dimensions.
  2. Each cell in the grid shows a letter label. Click cells to assign them to the same panel (merge) or reset them to individual panels.
  3. The mosaic is described as a 2D list of letters, e.g. [['A','A'],['B','C']] for a wide top panel over two equal bottom panels.

docs.title: Live preview
docs.text: A small preview thumbnail updates as you edit the mosaic, showing the resulting panel layout.

docs.title: Shared axes
docs.text:
Two checkboxes in the layout dialog configure axis sharing:

Option Effect Share X axis All subplots in the same column share their X limits and tick marks Share Y axis All subplots in the same row share their Y limits and tick marks

Shared axes keep panels visually aligned and make comparisons easier.

docs.title: Assigning series to subplots
docs.text:
In the Data tab series table, the Plot # column sets which subplot (1-based) a series appears in. Increment the number to move a series to a different panel.

The Axes and Legend & Notes tabs both have a Subplot selector at the top that lets you configure each panel independently. All three selectors (Axes, Legend & Notes, Series) stay in sync — changing one updates the others.

docs.title: Per-subplot settings
docs.text:
Each subplot has its own independent settings for:

  • Title text, font, size, and color
  • X, Y, and Y2 axis labels
  • Axis limits (auto or manual) for X, Y, and Y2
  • Axis scale (linear, log, logit, inverted)
  • Tick configuration (size, direction, minor ticks, rotation, step, formatter)
  • Legend (show/hide, position, style)
  • Annotation visibility
  • Canvas background, borders, grid and 3D view (Canvas & Grid tab)

Changes made in the Axes and Legend & Notes tabs always apply to the subplot currently shown in the selector.

When you add subplots, the new ones start with the look of the active subplot: fonts and sizes, tick and legend style, label layout, canvas colours and grid. What depends on the data (titles and labels, limits, scale, tick step, number format, chart type) starts empty or at its default.

docs.title: Transform
docs.text: The Data → Transform page creates new series from existing ones: smoothing, decimation, calculus, scaling, cleaning, resampling and signal analysis. To summarise series instead, see Statistics.

docs.title: The Transform page
docs.text:
The Transform page applies an operation (smoothing, decimation, calculus, scaling, cleaning, resampling…) to a series and stores the result as a new series. The original is never changed, so you can plot both together.

The Transform page:

  1. Series — x is the horizontal axis (optional) and y the series to transform.
  2. Operation — The operation, grouped by type, and its parameters, which change with the operation.
  3. Preview — What Apply would create, without creating anything. See Preview.
  4. Result — The name of the new series (automatic when empty) and the Apply button.

docs.title: Using it
docs.text:
1. x — the horizontal axis (for example the time or position series). Optional: choose (none: use index) when the series has no x column. Operations that need an x (resampling, cropping, sorting, aligning) report an error without it. Derivatives and integrals use the index as the spacing when there is no x.
  2. y — the series to transform (the values: the signal, the measurement). Swapping x and y gives odd results, because the result is calculated as a function of x: resampling y_irregular over t_irregular is a different curve from resampling t_irregular over y_irregular.
  3. Operation — pick it from the list, which is grouped by type (the group names are bold headers).
  4. Set the parameters, which change with the operation.
  5. Optionally type a Name for the result; the default is the series name plus a suffix, for example signal_MA5.
  6. Click Apply.

The status line under the button says what was created and how many points it has. New series appear at once in the Datasets list and in the series table.

docs.title: Preview
docs.text:
Below the parameters, a small plot shows what Apply would create, without creating anything: the original series in grey and the result on top of it. It uses the same calculation as Apply, so what you see is what you get.

  • Preview draws it once. Live (on by default) redraws shortly after any change — series, operation or parameter.
  • Peaks are drawn as markers. A spectrum is drawn alone, since its x axis is different. Date columns get a date axis. log y helps with spectra.
  • Long series are drawn with a reduced number of points (the highs and lows are kept). Above 50,000 points Live pauses; use Preview.
  • Problems (a window longer than the series, no x for a resample, ...) are written in the plot area instead of showing a dialog.
  • Under the plot, a line says how many points go in and the name of the series that would be created.

docs.title: Dates
docs.text:
When x is a date column, the operations that keep or select x values keep it as dates: the new x series from cropping, decimating, resampling, aligning, removing NaN or finding peaks is a date series, and plots with a date axis. Notes:

  • Crop x range: type the limits as dates, for example 2024-03-01 or 1 Mar 2024 12:00. Leave a box empty for no limit.
  • Resample (uniform x), derivatives, integrals and filters work in days: the derivative is per day, and the Butterworth cutoff is in cycles per day.
  • FFT amplitude spectrum: the frequencies are in cycles per day, and are not dates.
  • Moving average, median and the other window operations count points, not time, so they assume regular sampling; use Resample (uniform x) first if the dates are irregular.

Results are calculated once

A transformed series is a copy. If you later change or reload the original data, the transformed series is not recalculated — apply the operation again.

docs.title: When x changes
docs.text:
Some operations change the number or position of the points (decimating, cropping, resampling, removing NaN, FFT, peaks…). When that happens a new x series is created next to the new y, named after the x series and the suffix, for example t_every3 and y_every3. Plot the pair together.

  • FFT and Find peaks create their own x even if you chose none: frequencies for the FFT, and the x of each peak (the point index when there is no x series).
  • Align to another x reuses the x of the series you chose instead of creating a duplicate; the status line tells you which series to use as x.

docs.title: Smoothing
docs.text:
The same signal — a slow wave, a narrow bump at t = 7 s, a two-point spike and noise — smoothed six ways (grey: the original; orange: the result). The moving median ignores the spike, which the other filters turn into a bump. The moving average and Savitzky-Golay keep the height of the narrow bump best in this example; the Gaussian and the Butterworth filter round it off more.

Operation Parameters Notes Moving average Window, centered/trailing, ends Ends: partial averages the points that exist, nan leaves NaN where the window is incomplete, trim removes those points (and their x) Moving median Window Robust against isolated spikes; the window is rounded up to an odd number Exponential smoothing Alpha (0–1) s[i] = α·y[i] + (1−α)·s[i−1]; a smaller alpha smooths more Savitzky-Golay Window, polynomial order Local polynomial fit; keeps peak heights and widths better than a plain average. The order must be lower than the window Gaussian Sigma (in points) Gaussian kernel Low/high-pass filter (Butterworth) Type, cutoff, order Zero-phase. The cutoff is in cycles per x unit (cycles per point with no x) and must be below half the sampling rate. x should be evenly spaced and y must have no NaN

docs.title: Reduce and resample
docs.text:
A 0.4 Hz wave plus a 7.3 Hz one, sampled at 50 Hz, reduced to a tenth of the points. Every N points just keeps one point in ten, so the fast component is folded into a false slow wave (aliasing). Block average averages each block and lowers the amplitude. Decimate filters first, so only the real slow wave is left. The last panel shows unevenly spaced samples put on a uniform x grid with Resample.

Operation Parameters Notes Every N points N, start at Keeps one point out of every N Block average Block size Replaces each block by its mean, x included; a short last block is kept Resample (uniform x) Points, step Linear interpolation onto equally spaced x. Give a step (for example 0.001 for a sample every millisecond) to fix the spacing instead of the number of points; the step wins when both are set. Needs x Decimate (anti-aliased) Factor Low-pass filters first, then keeps every N-th point. y must have no NaN Align to another x Series, interpolation Interpolates y onto the x of another series (linear or pchip); NaN outside the range of the original x. Needs x Crop x range x min, x max Keeps x min ≤ x ≤ x max; leave a bound on auto to leave it open. Needs x

docs.title: Calculus
docs.text:
One smooth series (top left) and five operations on it. The derivative and the second derivative are its slope and curvature (the second derivative of 2 + sin t + 0.2t is −sin t). The cumulative integral is the area so far, starting at 0. Difference is the change from one point to the next, and Percent change the same relative to the previous value; the first point of both is NaN.

Operation Notes Derivative dy/dx Central differences Second derivative d2y/dx2 Needs at least 3 points Integral (cumulative) Trapezoid rule; the running total starts at the value you give in Starts at (the constant of integration, 0 by default) Difference y[i] − y[i−1]; the first point is NaN Percent change 100·(y[i] − y[i−1]) / abs(y[i−1]); the first point is NaN Log return ln(y[i] / y[i−1]); all values must be positive Cumulative sum Running total

docs.title: Scale and baseline
docs.text:
A series with an offset, a drift and a peak. Normalize rescales it to 0–1 (min-max) or to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 (z-score). Subtract baseline with mean of range takes a quiet stretch (x from 0 to 2) as the zero, which removes the offset but not the drift. Remove trend fits a straight line only on x from 0 to 4, before the peak, so that the peak does not tilt it, and subtracts it from the whole series. Scale and shift applies a·y + b.

Operation Parameters Notes Normalize Method min-max → 0 to 1; z-score → mean 0, std 1; first → divide by the first value; max → divide by the largest absolute value; value → divide by a number you type; mean of range → divide by the mean over an x range (for example the resting reading) Scale and shift a, b a·y + b Subtract baseline Baseline First value, last value, mean, median or minimum; a fixed value; or the mean / median of a range of x (a quiet stretch, so a peak does not pull the baseline up). The Value and x from / x to boxes appear only for the methods that use them; leave a limit empty to leave it open Absolute value — Remove trend (polynomial) Degree, fit from x, fit to x Subtracts a least-squares polynomial; degree 1 is a straight line. Limit the fit to a stretch of x (without the peak) so the peak does not tilt it; the result is subtracted over the whole series

docs.title: Cleaning
docs.text:
A series with two gaps (NaN) and three outliers; grey is the original. Remove NaN drops the missing points, so the line jumps across each gap, while Interpolate NaN keeps every point and fills the gaps linearly. Limit to a range clips the outliers to the limits. The Hampel filter replaces them by the local median and leaves the other points as they were. The last panel shows points that arrive out of order, and Sort by x putting them right.

Operation Parameters Notes Remove NaN — Drops points where y or x is NaN/inf, from both series Interpolate NaN — Fills gaps linearly using x (or the index); the ends hold the nearest valid value Limit to a range Lower, upper Clips y; leave a limit on auto to leave it open Sort by x — Reorders the points so x increases. Needs x Outlier filter (Hampel) Window, sigmas Replaces a point by the local median when it is more than sigmas robust standard deviations away from it

docs.title: Rolling statistics
docs.text:
A noisy signal. The rolling standard deviation shows where it varies most. The rolling minimum and maximum draw an envelope that follows the signal. The running minimum and maximum never go back: they are the smallest and largest values so far.

Operation Parameters Notes Rolling std deviation Window Centered; the ends use the points that exist Rolling minimum / maximum Window Same Running minimum / maximum — Cumulative: the smallest or largest value so far

docs.title: Signal analysis
docs.text:
Left: the spectrum of the 0.4 Hz plus 7.3 Hz signal above, with one line at each frequency and the amplitudes 1 and 0.5. Right: Find peaks on the pulse_signal.csv sample, with the threshold set to 5 times the noise, finds the two pulses and nothing in the noise.

Operation Parameters Notes FFT amplitude spectrum Remove mean Single-sided amplitude. x gives the sampling interval, so it should be evenly spaced; y must have no NaN. Output: frequency and amplitude Find peaks Min height (× noise), min height, min prominence, min distance Local maxima. Output: only the peak points. Min height (× noise) sets the threshold at the median plus k times the noise of the series (estimated robustly, so a few peaks do not inflate it; remove any drift first). With Min height as well, the higher limit applies. Prominence is measured against the valleys around a peak, so with noise it needs about 8 times the noise level; a height threshold of about 5 times is simpler. An error is shown if there are no peaks

Recipes

  • Remove spikes, then smooth: Outlier filter (Hampel), then Savitzky-Golay on the result.
  • Find the dominant frequency: Remove trend, then FFT amplitude spectrum, and plot the spectrum.
  • Uneven sampling: Resample (uniform x) before a Butterworth filter or an FFT.
  • Pulse in a stable signal with noise: Subtract baseline (median of range, over a stretch without the pulse), then Savitzky-Golay with a window no longer than the pulse (in points), then Find peaks with Min height (× noise) of 5 or 6 and a Min distance of the pulse width. Do not use the moving median or the outlier filter: they treat the pulse as noise and remove it. For a negative pulse, Scale and shift with a = −1 first.
  • Compare two series with different x: Align to another x puts one on the x of the other.
